text: Namecheap hosting suits small WordPress sites on a tight budget, but only if you plan for the renewal price. Stellar costs $1.88 a month on a 2-year term, then $4.29 a month when it renews. This Namecheap hosting review covers the three shared plans: Stellar (3 sites), Stellar Plus and Stellar Business (both unlimited sites). I run my own sites on Namecheap shared hosting, and I say so where that experience applies. Prices were checked on October 16, 2026 on Namecheap’s US shared hosting page and help center. Speed and uptime figures come from three outside tests, named in the table with their periods. Namecheap hosting plans and the real cost Every plan starts with a 30-day free trial, then a discounted rate on yearly or 2-year billing. Namecheap’s fine print says the discount does not apply to renewals. The plan page shows monthly rates only, so the term totals in the second table are my calculation (rate times months). Stellar Plus goes from $2.28 to $6.10 a month, 2.7 times. Moving from Stellar to Stellar Plus adds $53.16 over four years. Month-to-month billing is the costly route: Stellar at $5.88 for 48 months comes to $282.24, which is $134.24 more than the 2-year path. Month 24 is the point to compare prices again, and moving a site is a routine job: see how to move a WordPress site to a new host . Check Namecheap plans What Namecheap hosting includes, and the limits that matter Sites: Stellar allows 3 websites. Stellar Plus and Stellar Business are unlimited. For anyone building several affiliate sites, the fourth site is what pushes you from Stellar to Stellar Plus. Stellar also caps subdomains at 30 and mailboxes at 30, while the other two plans list both as unlimited. For separate business mailboxes, see our Namecheap email hosting review. Storage and files: Stellar has 20 GB SSD, Stellar Plus lists unmetered SSD and Stellar Business has 50 GB SSD. The file limit (inodes) is 300,000 on Stellar and Stellar Plus and 600,000 on Stellar Business, so “unmetered” on Stellar Plus is capped by file count, not by gigabytes. Namecheap also says the unmetered space is for your website only and falls under its Acceptable Use Policy. Free domain: every plan lists a free domain for the first year. Premium domains are excluded, and the fine print allows one domain per hosting plan. Server resources: Namecheap’s resource-limits page (updated June 24, 2026) gives a baseline shared account 1 GB of RAM and 20 entry processes, the number of requests the account can run at once. Stellar Plus is listed at 2 GB and 30. Stellar Business is listed at 2 GB, 40 entry processes and a 100% CPU limit, against 50% for the other columns. The page does not name Stellar separately, so the baseline is the closest figure for it. If a site outgrows these limits, our Namecheap VPS hosting review covers the next step up. Backups: the plan page says twice a week on every plan, plus AutoBackup on Stellar Plus and Stellar Business. AutoBackup keeps 6 daily, 3 weekly and 5 monthly copies for up to six months, and you cannot force one. An undated Namecheap help page says shared accounts get weekly backups for server restoration only, tells customers to keep their own copies, and says backups are made only for accounts of 25 GB or less and 200,000 files or fewer. That does not match the plan page, so keep a copy of your own. Security and extras: every plan lists Imunify360 (malware scanning and a firewall), automatic SSL installation, cPanel two-factor login and the Supersonic CDN, which Namecheap describes as built-in DDoS protection. A dedicated IP is an extra $4.00 a month. Staging: the shared plan page I read lists no staging tool. Data center: the US option is on the order page. Namecheap says its Cloud Storage layer comes with the US data center only on Stellar Business; on Stellar and Stellar Plus it is limited to the EU and Singapore locations. Namecheap hosting review: speed and uptime evidence Namecheap advertises a 100% uptime guarantee on all its shared plans. That is a provider claim, not a measured result. Its uptime guarantee terms give one free day of hosting for each hour of unplanned downtime, up to one month, if you open a billing ticket within 10 calendar days, and Namecheap alone decides whether an outage qualifies. Over a year, 99.89% is about 9.6 hours of downtime (8,760 hours times 0.11%), and 99.98% is about 1.8 hours. The speed figures use different methods (a 19 ms server response in one test, a 461 ms average TTFB in another), so they cannot be ranked against each other. Only one test names its plan. A single event can outweigh a year of small outages: the August 2026 Phoenix data center failure, covered in our Namecheap outage breakdown , took hosting down for about a day. Support and migration Namecheap lists live chat 24/7. I find its online support fast, and it emails me before it makes changes or updates on its side. Outside reviewers disagree: Kripesh Adwani found chat quick but not always helpful with hosting questions, and Gaurav Tiwari (updated June 2026) calls it slow to respond. Cybernews lists no phone support. If you are locked out rather than waiting on a reply, our guide to a Namecheap account locked lists which Namecheap email address handles each problem. Namecheap says migration from another cPanel host is free, with manual transfers possible case by case. That is the provider’s claim; I have not used it. On the setup side, I add new domains in cPanel and install WordPress with the one-click installer, and the control panel and file layout are easy to follow. Adding each new site takes a few minutes, as our step-by-step guide to adding a domain in cPanel shows. Moving a domain is a separate step, explained in our guide to transferring a domain to Namecheap . title: NameCheap Hosting Review (2026): Best Affordable Web Host

text: I have been on and off with Namecheap since 2015, moving between shared hosting and EasyWP-managed WordPress over the years. Most recently, I put the Stellar shared hosting plan through a proper test on one of my own live sites, tracking server behavior, cPanel features, SSL setup, and real TTFB numbers across 40 global test locations, rather than relying on a single speed check from one city. This Namecheap hosting review pulls from that firsthand testing. I am not going to repeat the generic “Namecheap is cheap and beginner-friendly” line you can find on every other hosting blog. Instead, I am going to walk you through exactly what you get in cPanel, where the SSL setup can quietly cost you money in year two, what the server actually does under load, and which of the three Stellar plans makes sense depending on what you are building. By the end, you should know whether Stellar shared hosting is the right call for your project or whether you are better off looking elsewhere. NameCheap Namecheap is one of the oldest and most popular domain name registrars and web hosts, known for its affordable hosting plans. But is it the right option for you? Find out all the answers in this in-depth review of Namecheap hosting from personal experience. Price: 1.78 Price Currency: USD Operating System: Web Application Category: BusinessApplication Editor's Rating: 4.01 Quick Verdict Namecheap’s Stellar shared hosting is a solid, budget-friendly starting point for a small site, a portfolio, or a first blog, especially now that you can try it free for 30 days before paying anything. Where it falls short is performance out of the box. There is no built-in caching layer, and without a CDN in front of your site, TTFB is on the slow side, particularly for visitors outside North America. If you are technical enough to layer a CDN on top and manage your own SSL renewal, Stellar is genuinely good value. If you want fast performance the moment you sign up, with zero extra configuration, you will want to budget for a CDN add-on from day one, or consider a managed WordPress host instead. Visit Namecheap The 30-Day Free Trial and How Namecheap’s Plans Are Structured The biggest change since I last reviewed Namecheap in depth is the free trial. Namecheap now lets you test its shared hosting free for 30 days before you commit a dollar. That is a meaningful shift from the old model, where you had to buy in advance and rely on a money-back guarantee if things did not work out. With the trial, you can see your site running on Namecheap’s infrastructure in your cPanel account before any billing kicks in. Once the trial period ends, you choose how you want to pay: monthly, annually, or every two years (biannual). Paying monthly gives you the most flexibility if you are not sure you want to stay long-term, but it also comes with the highest effective rate. Paying annually or biannually locks in a lower monthly cost but ties you in for longer, so weigh that against how confident you are in the platform before you commit to a multi-year term. Namecheap sells three tiers of Stellar shared hosting: Stellar, Stellar Plus, and Stellar Business. I will break down the pricing and the differences in detail further down, but the short version is that they are built for different stages of a website’s life, not just different budgets. The cPanel and Software Experience Namecheap’s shared hosting runs on the LiteSpeed web server, and that shows up throughout the cPanel experience in ways that matter if you have used other hosts before. Softaculous is included, which means one-click installs for WordPress and most other common CMS platforms work exactly as you would expect. If you have ever set up a WordPress site in cPanel, there is no learning curve here. What you will not find is WP Toolkit. If you’re usued to installing WordPress, controlling updates, staging environments, and site cloning from a single WP Toolkit dashboard on another host, that convenience simply is not part of the Stellar experience. Namecheap’s Softaculous is also powerful, and include most site management basic tool: staging, clone, update, backup, one-click retore, and more. For me, the difference between WP Toolkit and Softaculous is not which is better, but in philosophy and design. However, Namecheap does not include built-in Redis support engine on the server. For a personal blog or a small business site, this rarely matters. But if you are running WooCommerce , a membership site, or anything with heavier database queries and object caching needs, the absence of Redis is worth knowing about before you commit, because you will either need to work around it with a plugin-based caching solution or accept slower dynamic page loads. Auto-SSL vs Let’s Encrypt This is where I want to slow down, because it is the part of Namecheap hosting that catches people off guard the most. Namecheap does not offer free Let’s Encrypt SSL certificates, and I want to be precise about that because it might cause issues later. What Namecheap installs automatically is its own Auto-SSL certificate, and that Auto-SSL is only free for the first year. After twelve months, it renews as a paid product. That is a materially different arrangement than hosts that bundle Let’s Encrypt, which stays free indefinitely and auto-renews every 90 days without ever asking you to pay. The Auto-SSL install works cleanly and automatically if your domain is also registered with Namecheap. Domain and hosting live under the same account, and the certificate gets provisioned without you lifting a finger. If your domain is registered elsewhere, though, you need a workaround if you don’t want to use Namecheap Auto-SSL. The most reliable fix is to route your site through a CDN that installs SSL, such as Cloudflare or Quick.Cloud . Both of these will issue and manage SSL for your domain regardless of where it is registered, which sidesteps the Auto-SSL renewal cost entirely and, as a bonus, gets you a CDN layer that Namecheap’s shared hosting does not include out of the box. My advice: if you plan to stay on Namecheap shared hosting long term, decide on your SSL strategy on day one rather than getting surprised by a renewal charge in year two. AI Site-Building Tools One addition since I last covered Namecheap is that its now offer AI-powered site building tools included in cPanel. You get a choice between two: AI for WordPress is built for anyone who wants a WordPress site without touching a page builder manually. You start from a simple prompt describing your site, the AI generates it, and from there you use AI to edit pages, add content, manage changes, and troubleshoot common WordPress issues . This is the option to pick if you specifically want a WordPress backend under the hood, since it is generating and managing an actual WordPress install rather than a standalone site. Sitejet AI Website Builder takes a different approach. You choose between starter template selection or the AI website generator option. The AI generates your site from prompt, but instead of handing you WordPress, it drops you into a no-code editor where you fine-tune the layout, content, and design yourself. Namecheap positions this as the better fit if you want a more polished business website with more control over design, without needing to manually install WordPress at all. In my experience, both option works great, its just depend on conveniency and how much control you want. If you are launching a simple site fast and want a real starting point instead of a blank site, having both options built into cPanle is a genuine convenience Namecheap did not offer a couple of years ago. Performance and TTFB: The Real Numbers I ran a multi-run TTFB test across 40 global locations using SpeedVitals , on a Namecheap Stellar server with no optimization layered on top, meaning no CDN and no external caching. This matters, because a lot of Namecheap hosting reviews test with a CDN already in place and then credit the host for speed that is actually coming from Cloudflare or another edge network. I wanted to see what Namecheap’s own server delivers on its own. The results: Overall average TTFB: 723ms , which SpeedVitals graded an E (62%) Cache hit rate: none registered , confirming there is no built-in cache mechanism running by default Broken down by region, the picture gets more specific: North America averaged 418ms , the fastest region overall. The best-performing locations were Oregon at 191ms, Dallas at 215ms, and Northern Virginia at 253ms, all comfortably fast. But the region also had weak spots: Santiago, Chile came in at 1.1 seconds and São Paulo, Brazil at 949ms, both far outside acceptable range, while Montreal held a respectable 345ms. Europe averaged 597ms , solidly in the “needs improvement” zone. London led at 540ms, followed by Belgium at 545ms and Paris at 569ms. The slower end included Finland at 674ms, Warsaw at 662ms, and Sweden at 635ms. None of these are catastrophic, but none of them are fast either. Asia Pacific averaged 1.1 seconds , and this is where the server clearly struggles. Even the best-performing locations in the region were slow: Tel Aviv at 772ms, Tokyo at 886ms, and South Africa at 987ms. The worst regions were brutal: Delhi at 1.5 seconds, Jakarta at 1.4 seconds, and Mumbai at 1.2 seconds. If your audience is concentrated in North America or Western Europe, these numbers are workable, if not impressive. If you have any meaningful traffic from South America, South Asia, or Southeast Asia, these TTFB numbers will hurt your bounce rate and your Core Web Vitals scores, and you should plan to add a CDN from the start rather than treating it as optional. The one genuinely encouraging finding from this test had nothing to do with speed. On the account I was provisioned, server resource usage stayed healthy throughout testing: swap usage held consistently under 5%, and disk usage stayed consistently under 30%. That tells me the server I landed on was not overcrowded with other accounts fighting for the same CPU and RAM, which is a real risk on cheap shared hosting. I cannot promise every Namecheap server is provisioned this reasonably, but on my account, the “noisy neighbor” problem that plagues a lot of budget shared hosting was not something I ran into. Security Features Namecheap’s cPanel ships with a reasonable security stack for a shared hosting plan, and none of it requires a separate purchase or plugin to activate: SSH access , for anyone comfortable working from the command line ImunifyAV , for malware scanning Two-factor authentication (2FA) , to lock down your cPanel login itself Hotlink protection , to stop other sites from leeching your images and bandwidth IP blocker , for manually denying access to specific addresses or ranges ModSecurity , a web application firewall that filters malicious requests before they reach your site For a shared hosting tier, this is a fair set of tools. It will not match what you get on a managed WordPress platform with a dedicated firewall service, but it covers the basics that most small sites actually need. Support Support has consistently been one of Namecheap’s strongest points across every plan I have used, and that holds true here. Live chat responds almost instantly, day or night, and the reps I have dealt with clearly know the platform rather than reading from a script. If live chat cannot resolve something on the spot, you can escalate to an email ticket, and those get followed up on rather than disappearing into a queue. For a budget host, this is genuinely above what you would expect. Pricing: Which Stellar Plan Actually Fits You Namecheap’s shared hosting comes in three tiers, and the differences go beyond storage. Each one is built for a different kind of project. Stellar ($5.88/month, or $55.88/year with annual billing) is built for a single website or a very small handful of sites. It caps you at 3 websites, 20GB of SSD storage, and 30 mailboxes. If you are launching your first blog, a personal portfolio, or a single small business site and you do not need room to grow multiple domains under one account, this is the plan to start with. It is the plan I tested directly, and for a single-site setup with modest traffic, the resource allocation held up fine. Stellar Plus ($7.88/month, or $85.44/year with annual billing) removes the caps. You get unlimited websites, unmetered SSD storage, and unlimited mailboxes, plus AutoBackup included, which gives you automated daily, weekly, and monthly backups without configuring a third-party backup tool yourself. This is the plan that makes sense the moment you are managing more than one site, whether that is your own blog plus a side project, or a small agency setup hosting a few client sites under one account. The backup inclusion alone is worth the roughly $2 a month jump from Stellar if you are not already backing up manually. Stellar Business ($11.88/month, or $128.88/year with annual billing) adds 50GB of Cloud Storage instead of standard SSD, along with Imunify360 security bundled in at no extra cost, which layers on real-time malware scanning, automatic patching, and proactive bot and intrusion protection on top of the security stack I listed above. This tier is aimed at businesses that need better uptime assurances and stronger built-in security without manually piecing together a security stack, and it is the right call if your site handles anything sensitive, like customer data, logins, or e-commerce transactions, even at a small scale. Across all three tiers, you get some things bundled in regardless of which plan you pick: a 100% uptime guarantee, unmetered bandwidth, free website migration if you are moving from another host, and Namecheap’s own Supersonic CDN included for free. That last point matters given everything I said above about TTFB and third-party CDN. Namecheap’s Supersonic CDN is available on every Stellar tier, and turning it on is a genuinely smart move, but you must be using Namecheap’s nameservers to activate it. I haven’t tested their Supersonic CDN yet, since I prefer Cloudflare, due to its extensive network coverage (300+ edge locations) and a wide range of optimizations and security tools. If you are unsure which Namecheap Stellar plans to start with, my honest advice is this: start with Stellar if you are testing the waters with a single site, but move to Stellar Plus the moment you know you are staying, because the automated backups alone remove a real risk that a lot of new site owners do not think about until it is too late. Try Namecheap for 30 Day Pros and Cons Pros: 30-day free trial removes the risk of committing blind Genuinely responsive live chat and email support Server resources were not overcrowded on my account, with swap and disk usage staying low Solid built-in security stack (SSH, ImunifyAV, 2FA, Hotlink protection, IP blocker, ModSecurity) Free Supersonic CDN included on every plan, which can offset the weak default TTFB Competitive pricing across all three tiers, especially Stellar Plus for multi-site setups Cons: No built-in caching mechanism, so TTFB is slow out of the box, especially outside North America Auto-SSL is only free for the first year, then renews as a paid product No WP Toolkit for managing multiple WordPress installs from one dashboard No Redis support for sites with heavier database or object caching needs SSL setup gets more complicated if your domain is registered with a different registrar FAQs Is Namecheap shared hosting good for beginners? Yes, Namecheap is widely known as one of the best beginner-friendly web hosts. It offers marketing tools and a shared hosting plan suitable for people starting their first blog or for small- to medium-sized businesses running sites. Does Namecheap shared hosting include a free SSL certificate? Namecheap auto-installs its own Auto-SSL certificate, not Let’s Encrypt, and that Auto-SSL is only free for the first year. After that, it renews as a paid product. If your domain is registered with a different registrar, you will also need a workaround, such as routing through Cloudflare or Quick.Cloud, to get SSL installed cleanly. Is Namecheap shared hosting fast? Not out of the box. Testing the Stellar plan without a CDN or any caching layer resulted in an average TTFB of 723ms across 40 global locations and was graded an E by SpeedVitals. North American locations performed reasonably well, but Asia Pacific locations averaged over a full second. Turning on the free Supersonic CDN included with every plan meaningfully improves this, so it is worth enabling from day one rather than treating it as optional. Does Namecheap shared hosting support Redis or WP Toolkit? No. Neither Redis support nor WP Toolkit is available on Stellar shared hosting. Namecheap use Softacolous, and If your site handle heavier object caching, you will need a workaround or a different hosting plan, such as it VPS. How good is Namecheap’s customer support? It is one of the strongest parts of the hosting experience. Live chat responds almost instantly, and the reps I have dealt with generally understand the platform well. If live chat cannot resolve an issue, you can escalate to an email ticket, which gets followed up on rather than sitting in a queue. Does Namecheap offer a free trial?: Yes, Namecheap offer a 30 day free trial of its shared hosting plans: Stellar, Stellar Plus, and the Stellar Business plan. You don’t need to enter your payment information to get started. It’s free, and you just need to signup, pick a hosting plan, and start building immediately. Final Verdict Namecheap’s Stellar shared hosting is still what it has always been for me: an affordable, well-supported entry point that requires you to do a bit of homework to get the best out of it. The free trial makes it lower-risk than ever to test, and the quality of support is genuinely a differentiator from other budget hosts. But the raw performance numbers tell you exactly what you are paying for. A 723ms average TTFB with no built-in cache is not something you want to launch with and ignore, particularly if your audience is not concentrated in the US. My recommendation: if you pick Stellar or Stellar Plus, turn on the free Supersonic CDN from day one rather than treating it as a later optimization step, or decide upfront how you are handling SSL if your domain lives with another registrar. Handle those two things at setup, and Namecheap shared hosting is a genuinely solid, budget-friendly place to run a small site.

text: Namecheap Review 2026: The Go-To Domain Registrar That Also Does Hosting Founded: 2000 • Phoenix, Arizona, United States ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ 4.5 Starting at $1.98/mo 12 months contract, then $4.07/mo Reviewed by Jonathan Brown • ✓ Tested by us • Last verified: 03/05/2026 Visit Website → 🏷️ 5 Coupons TopSiteHosters may earn a commission if you sign up through links on this page. This doesn't affect the rating. Affiliate disclosure . Namecheap has a reputation that most hosting companies would kill for. Ask anyone in the WordPress community where to register a domain, and Namecheap comes up within the first three answers. Free privacy protection, competitive pricing, clean interface. As a domain registrar, it’s hard to beat at the budget end. In this article Quick Verdict What Is Namecheap? Shared Hosting Plans and Pricing EasyWP Managed WordPress Website Builder VPS Hosting Dedicated Servers Performance and Uptime Data Centres and European Hosting Security Features Customer Support Is Namecheap Good for Domains? Who Should Use Namecheap? Frequently Asked Questions Final Verdict The hosting side is a different story. Not a bad story, but a different one. Namecheap’s shared hosting and managed WordPress plans are affordable and functional, and they’re a natural choice if you already manage your domains there. They’re just not where the company’s real energy goes. This review covers both sides honestly, so you can decide whether to consolidate everything with Namecheap or split your domain registration and hosting between providers. We reviewed Namecheap’s shared hosting, EasyWP managed WordPress, and VPS plans as of March 2026, including pricing changes. We have tested Namecheap’s domain registration system firsthand. Hosting performance data in this review is drawn from independent third-party testing and verified user reports. Quick Verdict Namecheap is the right choice if you want a trusted, affordable domain registrar and are happy with solid, uncomplicated shared hosting in the same place. It’s a budget-friendly option for first sites, simple blogs, and small businesses that don’t need top-tier performance. Best for: First-time site owners, bloggers, and small businesses registering a domain and wanting hosting in one place. Also strong for anyone who values free domain privacy and competitive domain renewal pricing above all else. Not ideal for: Performance-focused WordPress sites, WooCommerce stores that need to handle traffic spikes, or anyone who relies on third-party caching plugins on their managed WordPress setup. What Is Namecheap? Namecheap was founded in 2000 by CEO Richard Kirkendall and is headquartered in Phoenix, Arizona. It’s an ICANN-accredited domain registrar , which means it can register, transfer, and manage domain names directly. Over two decades it has grown into one of the largest registrars in the world, now managing over 24 million domains for more than 10 million customers. The company is privately held. One note worth knowing if you’re considering EasyWP, their managed WordPress product: CVC Capital Partners, a private equity firm, acquired EasyWP in September 2025. The parent Namecheap brand remains independently operated, but the managed WordPress arm specifically has changed ownership. One sentence of context, not alarm. But it’s a fact most reviews haven’t mentioned, and readers making a long-term choice deserve to have it. Beyond domains and hosting, Namecheap offers SSL certificates, private email hosting, a VPN service called FastVPN, a CDN called Supersonic, and reseller hosting. It’s a full ecosystem for running a small web presence at a low price point. Shared Hosting Plans and Pricing Namecheap’s shared hosting sits under the Stellar branding and comes in three tiers. All plans include cPanel, free domain privacy (WhoisGuard), free SSL, unmetered bandwidth, a website builder, and a 30-day money-back guarantee . The table below shows both introductory and renewal rates, because the gap between the two is where most readers get caught out. Plan Storage Sites Intro (2yr) Intro (1yr) Renewal Stellar 20 GB SSD 3 only $1.58/mo $1.98/mo $4.07/mo Stellar Plus Unmetered Unlimited $2.48/mo $2.98/mo $6.24/mo Stellar Business 50 GB SSD Unlimited $4.48/mo $4.98/mo $9.41/mo The Stellar plan is worth a second look before you dismiss it as the obvious choice. It caps you at three websites, which is enough for most beginners but becomes limiting fast if you manage multiple projects. Stellar Plus is where the value really opens up: unlimited sites and unmetered storage for around $2.50/mo on a three-year term. Stellar Business adds an automated backup tool, which sounds minor until you need it. The basic two-tier plans give you backups twice a week rather than daily, and restore is not guaranteed on entry plans. For anyone running a site with regular content updates or e-commerce, the automated daily backup on Stellar Business is the right call. One note for European readers: hosting on a UK data centre costs an extra $1/mo or about $12/yr on top of your plan price. It’s worth it if your audience is primarily in the UK, since it reduces the distance between your server and your visitors, which shows up in load times. The UK, Amsterdam, and Singapore data centres all run on 100% renewable energy, which Namecheap doesn’t shout about much but is worth knowing. Renewal prices more than double on the 3-year intro rate once your first term is up. That’s not unusual in the hosting industry, but the gap is wider here than with some competitors. The renewal rates themselves are reasonable at $3.88 to $9.88/mo. Just factor them in before you sign up. EasyWP Managed WordPress EasyWP is Namecheap’s managed WordPress platform, and it’s a distinct product from their shared hosting. It uses a custom dashboard rather than cPanel, it runs on Namecheap’s own cloud infrastructure, and it’s built specifically for WordPress with no other CMS supported. There are three tiers, each covering a single WordPress installation. Plan Storage CPU/RAM Monthly Rate Free Domain Starter 10 GB NVMe Base $9.88/mo No Turbo 50 GB NVMe 1.5x $13.88/mo Yes (yearly plan) Supersonic 100 GB NVMe 2x $20.88/mo Yes (yearly plan) One thing to flag upfront: the Starter plan previously cost $3.88/mo. Since August 2025, that price increased to $9.88/mo. Most reviews you’ll find online still show the old figure. The pricing above reflects what you’ll actually pay today. EasyWP’s dashboard is clean and stripped back. You get site creation, backups, SSL, domain connection, and traffic stats. What you don’t get is the full depth of cPanel . For a beginner who just wants WordPress running, that’s fine. For anyone who wants to install third-party caching plugins like WP Rocket or W3 Total Cache, this is where EasyWP becomes a problem: those plugins are disabled on the platform. Namecheap uses its own caching layer, which works, but you can’t swap it out for something you prefer or are already familiar with. Backups are another thing to check carefully. The Starter plan has manual backups only. If you forget to back up and something goes wrong, there’s no automatic restore point. Turbo and Supersonic include automated backups. For any site you care about, Turbo should be the minimum. Free domain and free business email are included with Turbo and Supersonic on yearly plans. The free domain covers a range of TLDs at no cost (.me, .online, .site, and others), with .com and .net available at a 60% discount. RelateSEO, their SEO tool, is bundled free for three months on yearly Turbo and Supersonic plans. On performance: EasyWP has recorded 100% uptime in independent monitoring. The concern is traffic spikes. In load testing, EasyWP recorded a 56.80% error rate under concurrent traffic . If your site has unpredictable traffic, or if you’re building something that could go viral or run a flash sale, EasyWP’s infrastructure may not hold up reliably. For steady, moderate-traffic WordPress blogs and small business sites, it performs fine. Website Builder Namecheap includes two website builder options depending on which hosting product you’re on. On shared hosting plans, you get access to both an AI Website Builder and Sitejet. The AI builder is the simpler of the two, you answer a few questions about your business, pick a template, and it generates a basic site. It’s aimed at complete beginners who want something live quickly without touching code. Sitejet sits a step up, offering more control over layout and design, and is particularly suited to web designers or agencies building sites for clients. It supports responsive design tools and client collaboration features, which makes it more useful as a professional tool than a beginner shortcut. On EasyWP managed WordPress plans, Turbo and Supersonic include the Brizy site builder. Brizy is a block-based drag-and-drop builder that works within WordPress. It’s more capable than the AI builder and gives you proper page layout control without needing to write code. Starter does not include Brizy. None of these replace a full page builder like Elementor or a dedicated website builder platform like Squarespace. But for a hosting provider including them at no extra cost, the selection is reasonable. If you are starting from scratch and just need something functional, the AI builder or Sitejet will get you there. If you are building a WordPress site and want design flexibility, Brizy on Turbo or Supersonic is the better route. VPS Hosting Namecheap offers three main VPS plans, all Linux-based with full root access, SSD RAID 10 storage, and a choice of operating system (AlmaLinux, Ubuntu, or Debian). Plan CPU RAM Storage Bandwidth Monthly Renewal Spark 1 core 1 GB 20 GB SSD RAID 10 1 TB $3.88/mo $4.88/mo Pulsar 2 cores 2 GB 40 GB SSD RAID 10 1 TB $6.88/mo $8.88/mo Quasar 4 cores 6 GB 120 GB SSD RAID 10 3 TB $12.88/mo $15.88/mo Magnetar 8 cores 12 GB 240 GB SSD RAID 10 6 TB $24.88/mo $28.88/mo Hypernova 12 cores 24 GB RAM 500 GB SSD RAID 10 10 TB $46.88/mo $52.88/mo Two things to know before you pick a plan. First, cPanel is not included. It’s a paid add-on at $17.88/mo, which is a meaningful extra cost on top of an already affordable plan. Webuzo is available at $2.88/mo as a lighter alternative. Second, the Pulsar plan only supports unmanaged (user-responsible) server management. If you want Namecheap’s team to handle server maintenance and updates, you need Quasar or above. The bandwidth allocations are on the conservative side compared to some competitors. If you expect high traffic volumes, compare these limits against what providers like Hostinger or Hetzner offer at similar price points before committing. For VPS hosting in general, Namecheap is competitively priced at the entry level, but the hardware specs are not as modern as some dedicated VPS-focused hosts. Dedicated Servers Namecheap offers dedicated servers for users who need an entire physical machine rather than a shared or virtualised environment. These are unmanaged by default and hosted in the Phoenix, Arizona data centre. The range spans entry-level single-processor servers through to dual-processor configurations with NVMe storage . Here is the current lineup at yearly billing rates: Server CPU RAM Storage Bandwidth Yearly Price Xeon E3-1230 v5 4 cores @ 3.4 GHz 8 GB DDR4 480 GB SSD 100 TB/mo $37.66/mo Xeon E-2136 6 cores @ 3.3 GHz 32 GB DDR4 2x 480 GB SSD 100 TB/mo $56.52/mo Dual Xeon Silver 4208 2×8 cores @ 2.1 GHz 64 GB DDR4 2x 1 TB NVMe Unmetered $135.41/mo Dual Xeon Gold 5218 2×16 cores @ 2.3 GHz 128 GB DDR4 4x 1 TB NVMe Unmetered $160.64/mo Dedicated servers are not the right choice for most readers on this site. They require technical knowledge to configure and maintain, and the US-only data centre location means European businesses will not benefit from the reduced latency that makes dedicated servers worth the cost. For high-traffic sites needing dedicated resources in Europe, providers like Hetzner offer a stronger hardware-to-price ratio with EU-based infrastructure. That said, if you are already managing your domains and hosting with Namecheap and need to step up to a dedicated environment, keeping everything under one account has its own convenience value. Prices shown are introductory yearly billing rates. Renewal rates are higher, verify current pricing at checkout. Performance and Uptime Namecheap’s shared hosting performs well for the price. In independent testing, a WordPress test site recorded a TTFB of 232ms, an LCP of 526ms, and a total blocking time of 21ms. GTmetrix gave a 100% performance score. All of those figures sit comfortably within Google’s Core Web Vitals good thresholds. Uptime held at 99.95% over a 30-day monitoring period in one independent test, and Namecheap claims 100% uptime on shared plans with compensation if they miss it. In practice, the occasional outage does occur, but it’s rare and typically brief. You can check how much downtime a 99.9% or 100% guarantee actually translates to using the uptime calculator . Shared hosting runs on a mix of Apache and LiteSpeed servers, which contributes to the solid speed figures. The caveat is location: performance is strong for US and EU visitors, but noticeably slower for audiences in Asia or other regions without a CDN in place. In one test, loading from a US server to a Bangalore connection took over four seconds. If your audience is global, activating the free Supersonic CDN tier helps, though the free version caps at 50 GB/mo traffic. You can test your own server’s response time from multiple global locations using the server response tester once you’re set up. Data Centres and European Hosting Namecheap has four data centre locations: Phoenix (Arizona, USA), Nottingham and Farnborough (UK), Amsterdam (Netherlands), and Singapore. The UK, EU, and Singapore locations all run on 100% renewable energy, which isn’t something Namecheap promotes heavily but is worth knowing if sustainability factors into your supplier decisions. For shared hosting, you choose your data centre at signup. The UK data centre costs an extra $1/mo on top of your plan price, which is reasonable if your audience is primarily in the UK or Ireland. The Amsterdam location covers mainland Europe well. VPS and dedicated server plans are currently US only, hosted in Phoenix. To host on a EU data centre, you need to select a 2-year billing plan for shared hosting. Monthly and 1-year plans are US-only. Choosing the right location matters more than most people expect. Hosting a UK-focused site on a US server adds physical latency every time a visitor loads a page. It’s rarely dramatic at small traffic volumes, but it does affect your Core Web Vitals scores and, over time, your search rankings. Security Features All Namecheap plans include free SSL certificates from Sectigo, automatically installed and covering up to 50 websites on shared hosting plans. You can check the SSL status of your current site with the SSL checker before you migrate. WhoisGuard, Namecheap’s domain privacy service, is included free with domain purchases. This hides your personal details from the public WHOIS record, preventing spam and protecting your identity. Most registrars charge $10–15/yr for this. Namecheap includes it at no cost, and it’s one of the strongest reasons to use them specifically for domain registration. Other security features across plans include ModSecurity for basic traffic filtering, two-factor authentication at the account level, and basic DDoS protection through the free Supersonic CDN tier. An advanced Web Application Firewall is available on paid Supersonic CDN plans. VPS plans come with software firewalls and a security package built into the infrastructure. Customer Support Namecheap offers 24/7 support through live chat and ticketing. There is no phone support, which is quite a gap for business users who want to talk to someone when something breaks urgently. The live chat response time is generally fast, and the knowledge base is well-regarded and comprehensive. During peak periods, ticket responses can take several hours, which has been a recurring complaint in user reviews. Shopper Approved gives them a 4.7 out of 5 rating, which is strong across a large volume of reviews. Priority support is only available on EasyWP Supersonic. On all other plans, including shared hosting and the lower EasyWP tiers, you’re in the same queue as everyone else. Is Namecheap Good for Domains? Yes. This is the honest answer, and it’s worth saying clearly. Namecheap’s domain product is one of the best at the budget end of the market. Free WhoisGuard privacy is included as standard, which competitors charge separately for. Renewal pricing is competitive and transparent, something Namecheap shows upfront rather than hiding until checkout. The Beast Mode bulk search tool lets you search hundreds of domain ideas at once, which is useful if you’re building a portfolio of sites. PremiumDNS is available as a paid add-on at around $5/yr, adding DNS failover and faster global propagation for sites where DNS reliability matters. The domain marketplace lets you buy and sell domains directly on the platform, and there’s FreeDNS for domains hosted elsewhere that need Namecheap’s DNS infrastructure. For anyone building a web presence from scratch, registering the domain at Namecheap and hosting elsewhere is a completely valid approach. The hosting is good. The domain product is great. Those are different things. You can check if your domain is available before registering with Namecheap Who Should Use Namecheap? Namecheap works well for a specific type of user, and it’s worth being direct about who that is. It’s a good fit if you’re: Registering a domain and want affordable hosting in the same place Building a first website, personal blog, or small business site that won’t see huge traffic Based in the UK or EU and want data centre options with green energy credentials Running multiple simple sites and want the value of Stellar Plus’s unlimited plan A developer or agency that wants clean domain management at scale It’s probably not the right call if you’re: Running a WooCommerce store or any site that needs to handle traffic spikes reliably. EasyWP’s load test results are a concern here Someone who relies on third-party caching plugins. EasyWP blocks them Looking for managed WordPress with a strong performance track record. Hostinger or SiteGround are better fits at similar price points A developer who needs a modern, spec-heavy VPS. Providers like Hetzner or Scala Hosting offer more hardware for the money at the VPS level The sweet spot for Namecheap is the user who wants simplicity, a trusted registrar, and hosting that just works without costing much. For that person, it delivers. Frequently Asked Questions Is Namecheap good for WordPress hosting? It depends on which product you use. The shared hosting plans run LiteSpeed servers and perform well for standard WordPress sites, with TTFB around 230ms in independent tests. EasyWP is more convenient but restricts third-party caching plugins and struggled under load testing with concurrent traffic. For a simple blog or small business site, either works fine. For a WooCommerce store or a site expecting traffic surges, look at alternatives like Hostinger or SiteGround. Does Namecheap include cPanel? Yes, on shared hosting and VPS plans. All three Stellar shared hosting plans include cPanel at no extra cost. On VPS plans, cPanel is a paid add-on at $17.88/mo. EasyWP uses a custom dashboard and does not include cPanel at all. Does Namecheap include free domain privacy? Yes. WhoisGuard, Namecheap’s domain privacy protection, is included free with domain registrations. This hides your personal information from the public WHOIS database. Most registrars charge $10–15/yr for this. Namecheap includes it as standard, which is one of the clearest reasons to use them specifically as a registrar. What is EasyWP and is it worth it? EasyWP is Namecheap’s managed WordPress hosting platform. It runs on Namecheap’s own cloud infrastructure, uses a simplified custom dashboard instead of cPanel, and handles WordPress setup, updates, and SSL automatically. It’s convenient for beginners who want WordPress running without technical setup. The limitations worth knowing: the Starter plan only has manual backups, third-party caching plugins are blocked, and the platform has shown error rates under high concurrent traffic in independent testing. For a low-traffic blog or small business site, it’s worth considering. For anything more demanding, compare it carefully against alternatives before committing. How does Namecheap compare to Hostinger? Hostinger is faster, more generous with storage, and performs better under load. Namecheap wins on domain pricing, free WhoisGuard privacy, and simplicity for users who want everything under one roof. If raw hosting performance is the priority, Hostinger edges it. If domain management and keeping costs low across multiple domains is the priority, Namecheap has the stronger case. See the full Hostinger review for a direct breakdown. Final Verdict Namecheap has built something extremely useful: a domain registrar that most people trust, combined with hosting that’s affordable and uncomplicated. The shared Stellar plans are honest value. The EasyWP platform is convenient for beginners, though the recent price increase and the caching plugin restrictions are real things to weigh before signing up. The domain product is the standout. Free privacy, transparent renewal pricing, and clean management tools at a budget price point. If you’re registering a domain, Namecheap belongs on the shortlist. If you’re choosing hosting on its own merits, it’s a solid option for simple sites and less compelling for anything performance-critical. For most readers on this site, the best approach is straightforward: use Namecheap for your domain if price and privacy matter, and make a separate hosting decision based on what your site actually needs.
